result: Mismatched BMSCs are necessary and sufficient to induce fibrosis in a dose-dependent manner. Depletion of BMSCs from whole bone marrow transplants rescues mice from fibrosis and lacrimal gland dysfunction, while recipients of mismatched HSCs with syngeneic BMSCs show no disease.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C16-C17, C20-C23, C74-C76, and C105 collectively demonstrate that mismatched BMSCs are both necessary and sufficient for disease induction. The data show progressive fibrosis only in mismatched BMSC recipients (C16), dose-dependent severity (C23, C76), rescue by BMSC depletion (C2, C22, C74-C75, C105), and lack of disease with mismatched HSCs plus syngeneic BMSCs (C17). Multiple organs show consistent patterns with statistical significance and appropriate controls.

result: Donor-derived fibroblasts in fibrotic lesions originate from transplanted BMSCs, not HSCs. Approximately 42.9±7.3% of HSP47+ fibroblasts are donor BMSC-derived, with no HSP47+ cells derived from donor HSCs. Donor BMSCs migrate to target organs and proliferate under pathological conditions.
evaluation: Claims C24-C32, C93-C94 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (immunofluorescence with GFP+ cells, in vitro culture, lineage tracing) demonstrating BMSC origin of fibroblasts. The quantitative data (C24: 42.9±7.3% GFP+HSP47+) is supported by appropriate controls showing no HSP47+ cells from HSCs (C26, C31) and no accumulation in syngeneic transplants (C28). The interpretation that this represents 'majority' (C25) is questionable given 42.9% is less than 50%, but the overall conclusion of BMSC contribution is well-supported.

result: Host T cells, not donor T cells, are required for fibrosis progression. Disease does not occur in T-cell-deficient nude mice recipients, nor in RAG2KO recipients lacking host T cells, but does occur when RAG2KO donor HSCs (lacking donor T cells) are transplanted with mismatched BMSCs into wild-type recipients.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C39-C40, C8, and C101 demonstrate through complementary genetic approaches that host T cells are necessary for disease. The use of nude mice (C33-C34), RAG2KO recipients (C39), and RAG2KO donors (C40, C8) provides strong evidence excluding donor T cell involvement. The experimental design appropriately controls for T cell origin, though the claim about 'radio-resistant residual recipient T cells' (C101) requires additional validation of T cell chimerism kinetics.

result: Mismatched BMSC transplantation induces recipient-derived Th17 cells in proximity to donor BMSCs. Donor BMSCs produce IL-6, and CD4+IL-17+ cells comprise >50% of splenic cells when mismatched BMSCs are transplanted with RAG2KO HSCs. Th17 cell increases are observed in both mismatched WBMT and BMSC groups.
evaluation: Claims C41-C45, C48-C49, C71-C72, and C77 demonstrate Th17 induction through multiple methods (immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, ELISA). The spatial proximity of Th17 cells to donor BMSCs (C41), IL-6 production by BMSCs (C42), and dramatic increase in Th17 cells with RAG2KO donors (C44: >50%) provide strong mechanistic evidence. The temporal differences between WBMT and BMSC transplantation (C72) add important kinetic information. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

result: Mismatched BMSC transplantation suppresses the transient increase in regulatory T cells (Tregs) that normally occurs after syngeneic transplantation. CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ Tregs transiently increase at 3 weeks after syngeneic transplantation but this increase is absent after mismatched BMSC or WBM transplantation.
evaluation: Claims C5, C68-C70, and C77 demonstrate Treg suppression through flow cytometry analysis at multiple time points. The comparison between syngeneic (showing transient increase at 3 weeks) and mismatched transplantation (no increase) is statistically significant (C69-C70). This finding is mechanistically consistent with IL-6-mediated Treg suppression and provides important evidence for autoimmune disease onset (C77). The temporal dynamics are well-characterized.

result: Adoptive transfer of T cells from mismatched BMSC-transplanted recipients into naive nude mice induces inflammation and fibrosis in target organs. These transferred T cells have acquired autoreactive properties and can induce disease independent of donor BMSCs.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49, C9, C82-C84 demonstrate through adoptive transfer experiments that T cells from diseased mice are sufficient to induce disease in naive recipients. The increased HSP47+ fibroblasts (C47), elevated Th17 cells (C48), and increased serum IL-17 (C49) in recipient nude mice provide strong evidence. This establishes that once T cells are activated by mismatched BMSCs, they maintain autoreactive properties (C9, C84). The experimental design appropriately uses nude mice to avoid confounding by recipient T cells.

result: T cells from mismatched BMSC-transplanted recipients proliferate and produce IL-6 when co-cultured with BMSCs but not dendritic cells. These T cells also respond to syngeneic (BALB/c) BMSCs, suggesting acquisition of autoreactive properties via antigen spreading.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 and C80 demonstrate T cell activation by BMSCs through in vitro co-culture experiments with appropriate controls (DCs, naive T cells). The proliferation (C52, C80) and IL-6 production (C53, C57) are well-documented with BrdU assays and ELISA. The response to syngeneic BMSCs (C54) supports antigen spreading (C55), though this interpretation relies on a single citation and would benefit from additional mechanistic validation. The specificity for BMSCs over DCs is an important control.

result: BMSCs act as antigen-presenting cells via MHC class II molecules. T cell proliferation is blocked by anti-MHC class II antibody, CD4+ T cells predominate over CD8+ T cells, and MHC class II expression on BMSCs increases significantly after co-culture with recipient T cells.
evaluation: Claims C3, C58-C63, and C81 provide strong evidence for BMSC antigen presentation through multiple complementary approaches: antibody blocking (C58, C81), T cell subset analysis (C59), and flow cytometry showing MHC class II upregulation (C61-C62). The predominance of CD4+ T cells (C59) and MHC class II dependence (C58) are consistent with classical antigen presentation. The increase in MHC class II expression after T cell co-culture (C62) suggests bidirectional activation. The conclusion that BMSCs present 'unknown but specific antigens' (C63) is appropriately cautious.

result: Serum IL-6 levels increase starting at 3 weeks after mismatched BMSC transplantation, coinciding with appearance of donor BMSCs in peripheral blood. A significant fraction of circulating BMSCs express MHC class II antigens after transplantation. These migrating donor BMSCs trigger increased IL-6, decreased Tregs, and increased Th17 cells.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66, C78, and C96 establish temporal correlation between BMSC mobilization, MHC class II expression, and IL-6 elevation through ELISA and flow cytometry. The kinetics (starting at 3 weeks, peaking at 7 weeks) are well-characterized (C65). The increase in MHC class II expression on circulating BMSCs (C66, C96) is an important observation, though the functional significance requires further validation. The proposed sequence of events (C78) is a reasonable interpretation but represents inference rather than direct demonstration of causality.

result: Minor antigen mismatched BMSCs trigger systemic fibrosis in this autoimmune scleroderma model through interaction with residual host T cells, inducing IL-6 production and leading to pathological changes similar to autoimmune disease. Accidental recognition of self-minor antigens on MHC class II+ BMSCs may be involved.
evaluation: Claims C10, C73, C112-C113, and C121 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These interpretations are well-supported by the collective evidence from transplantation experiments, T cell analyses, and mechanistic studies. The proposed mechanism involving minor antigen recognition (C113) is appropriately presented as speculative ('may be involved') since the specific antigen remains unidentified. The overall model integrating BMSC transplantation, T cell activation, IL-6 production, Treg suppression, and Th17 induction is consistent with all experimental observations.

result: The B10.D2 to BALB/c bone marrow transplantation model is an established MHC-compatible, minor histocompatibility antigen-incompatible model of systemic fibrosis. Fibrosis appears by 3 weeks and progresses to full-blown disease by 8 weeks, affecting multiple organs. The model occurs spontaneously without artificial agents.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C122-C124 describe the established mouse model with appropriate citations (Zhang et al., 2002; Yamamoto and Nishioka, 2004). The characterization of disease kinetics (3 weeks onset, 8 weeks full disease) and organ involvement is supported by histological data in supplementary figures. The model's spontaneous nature (C123) and similarity to human SSc (C124) are important validations. These claims appropriately cite prior work and are supported by the authors' confirmatory observations.

result: Prospectively isolated PαS-BMSCs express established BMSC markers CD29, CD90, and CD106, while endothelial markers CD31 and CD133 comprise only a small portion of the fraction.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15 provide essential characterization of the isolated BMSC population through flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C). The expression of established BMSC markers (C14) and minimal contamination with endothelial cells (C15) validates the cell isolation method. This characterization is critical for interpreting subsequent experiments but represents methodological validation rather than a primary finding.

result: HSP47 is a molecular chaperone specific to collagen-secreting cells and has been reported as a useful marker for fibroblasts in paraffin-embedded tissue sections.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 cite Kuroda and Tajima, 2004 for the characterization and application of HSP47 as a fibroblast marker. This represents appropriate use of established methodology from the literature. The authors apply this marker consistently throughout their study for quantifying fibrosis, which is a standard approach in the field.

result: Both host-derived and donor HSC-derived T cells exist in this model because mature T cells often escape radiation damage. Almost all spleen cells are donor-derived in matched WBMT, while more host-derived cells remain after mismatched WBMT.
evaluation: Claims C35-C38 describe T cell chimerism patterns with appropriate citation (Anderson et al., 2004) for the biological phenomenon of T cell radiation resistance. The observation of differential chimerism between matched and mismatched transplants (C37-C38) is supported by GFP analysis (Figure 2E). This provides important context for interpreting the role of host versus donor T cells, though the quantification could be more precise.

result: Recipient mature T cells act as effectors for mismatched BMSCs during fibrosis onset. It is unlikely that escape of donor-derived T cells from negative selection by the host thymus is involved in recognizing host tissue as non-self.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 represent interpretations of the experimental data. C50 is well-supported by the RAG2KO experiments and adoptive transfer studies. C51 is based on absence of EGFP+ BMSC-derived cells in the thymus, though this is stated as unpublished data ('data not shown'), which weakens the evidence. The conclusion is reasonable but would benefit from presentation of the supporting data.

result: Increased IL-6 during an autoimmune process leads to induction of Th17 cells and decrease in regulatory T cells (Tregs).
evaluation: Claim C67 cites Bettelli et al., 2006 for this established immunological mechanism. This represents appropriate use of prior knowledge to interpret the experimental observations. The authors' data on IL-6 elevation, Treg suppression, and Th17 induction are consistent with this established mechanism.

result: The autoantigen remains unidentified but is likely a common antigen expressed in BMSCs with different isoforms between strains. Autoreactive T cells present at basal levels can recognize minor differences between B10.D2 and BALB/c BMSCs. The phenotype is bidirectional (observed when strains are reversed).
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 represent speculation about the nature of the autoantigen. While the speculation is reasonable and consistent with the data, the key evidence is limited: C86 cites Sakaguchi et al., 2008 for basal autoreactive T cells, C87 infers from lack of HSC-induced disease, and C88 references unpublished data ('data not shown'). The bidirectional nature (C88-C89) is an important observation but lacks presented data. These claims appropriately acknowledge uncertainty but require additional experimental validation.

result: The novelty of this study is using prospectively isolated BMSCs combined with prospectively isolated HSCs, unlike previous studies using culture-isolated BMSCs. This approach allows selective transplantation of freshly isolated cell populations and addresses the unknown in vivo dynamics of BMSCs after transplantation.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 and C114-C120 establish the methodological advance and rationale for the study. The limitations of prior approaches using cultured BMSCs (C91, C115-C117) are well-documented with appropriate citations. The characterization of PαS-BMSCs (C119, citing Morikawa et al., 2009a,b) and the novel capability of the model (C120) are clearly stated. This represents an important methodological contribution that enables the key findings.

result: Donor BMSCs contribute to fibroblast populations in fibrotic lesions. Once mismatched BMSCs migrate to target organs, they encounter T cells and proliferate under pathological conditions. This phenomenon may not occur in syngeneic transplantation. Activation or maturation of BMSC-derived progeny is probably involved in disease progression.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 and C79 synthesize observations about BMSC behavior in vivo. C93 is well-supported by the lineage tracing data. C94 represents reasonable inference from the spatial localization and proliferation data, though direct demonstration of proliferation in vivo is limited. C95 and C79 are appropriately presented as speculation ('may not be present', 'probably involved') based on the absence of fibroblast accumulation in syngeneic transplants. These interpretations are consistent with the data but represent inference rather than direct demonstration.

result: Preliminary data show that MHC class II+ BMSCs in peripheral blood also express CD45 and type I collagen, corresponding with the phenotype of fibrocytes reported in the literature.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe preliminary unpublished data ('data not shown') with multiple citations for the fibrocyte phenotype. Without presentation of the actual data, it is impossible to evaluate the quality of evidence for CD45 and collagen expression. The correspondence with published fibrocyte phenotypes (C98) is an interesting hypothesis but requires validation. This represents an intriguing observation that warrants follow-up but cannot be fully evaluated without the supporting data.

result: This SSc model has been used as a cGVHD model. Unlike conventional cGVHD caused by donor T cells, residual recipient T cells are activated in this model. The reduced cGVHD risk in cord blood transplantation versus peripheral blood transplantation may correlate with BMSC content in grafts, and CD34+ selection may reduce cGVHD by depleting BMSCs.
evaluation: Claims C99-C104 and C106-C111 draw connections between the mouse model and clinical cGVHD. The citations for model use (C99: Kaplan et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2007), recipient T cell involvement (C102), and clinical observations (C103, C108) are appropriate. However, the speculation about BMSC content correlating with cGVHD risk (C110-C111) and the mechanism of CD34+ selection benefit (C107) represent extrapolation from mouse data to human disease. The authors appropriately note they 'do not believe that our findings in this mouse model could be directly applied to human cGVHD cases,' but then make these speculative connections. These claims require clinical validation and represent hypotheses rather than established findings.

result: Animal models are effective for screening therapeutic interventions. Spontaneous models are valuable tools for investigating SSc pathogenesis, which remains largely unknown. Systemic fibrosis is a feature of autoimmune diseases such as SSc and Sjögren's syndrome.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 provide background and rationale with appropriate citations. C125 cites specific therapeutic studies (Le Huu et al., 2012; Yaguchi et al., 2013), C127 cites clinical references (Ferrara et al., 2009; Filipovich et al., 2005), and C126 states the rationale for the study. These represent standard background information appropriately supported by literature citations.
